state.misconception_label: Thinks you can find missing values in a given table by treating the row as linear and adding on the difference between the first two values given.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The equation \( f=3 r^{2}+3 \) is used to find values in the table below. What is the value covered by the star? \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline\( r \) & \( 1 \) & \( 2 \) & \( 3 \) & \( 4 \) \\ \hline\( f \) & \( 6 \) & \( 15 \) & \( \color{gold}\bigstar \) & \\ \hline \end{tabular}. I got \( 24 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: What would happen if you tried your method on a simpler version of the problem?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, okay... so like, if I look at the first two values, 6 and 15, the difference is 9, right? So I added 9 to 15 to get 24. But I'm not really sure what you mean by a simpler version - do you mean like, using smaller numbers or something?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: What if you consider what the equation actually represents in this context? How does the equation \( f=3 r^{2}+3 \) relate to the values in the table?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, so like... the equation tells us how to *calculate* each value of f using the r value? So instead of just adding the difference, I should actually plug in the number 3 into the equation to get the star? But I'm still a bit confused about why just adding 9 each time doesn't work...

score.justification_pass1: The teacher prompts reasoning rather than direct correction, but doesn't explicitly address why linear addition fails for quadratic relationships, leaving the student still confused about their original method by Turn 4.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student toward understanding the equation rather than giving direct answers, though they could have more explicitly used a counterexample to expose the flawed pattern-based reasoning.
